title: WestJet Flight Attendants Issue Strike Notice, Threatening Peak Summer Travel
excerpt: Canada's second-largest airline faces a potential walkout starting August 2 after cabin crew issued a 72-hour strike notice over a dispute about unpaid work, with 75,000 passengers at risk.
body:
• WestJet flight attendants, represented by CUPE Local 8125, issued a 72-hour strike notice on July 30 over unpaid work disputes, with a walkout possible as early as August 2.
  • WestJet responded with its own 72-hour lockout notice but said it remains "encouraged by the progress" in negotiations.
  • An estimated 75,000 passengers could be affected if mass cancellations occur during peak summer travel.
  • Travelers with flights between July 30 and August 4 can rebook or cancel once without penalty; those who booked through third parties must contact their original agency.

Cabin Crew Issue Deadline as Talks Stall

WestJet flight attendants gave 72-hour notice for a strike on Wednesday, setting up a potential walkout during one of the busiest travel weekends of the Canadian summer. The Canadian Union of Public Employees (CUPE) said cabin crew at Canada's second-largest airline could walk off the job as early as August 2 at 12:01 a.m. Mountain Time if talks fail to produce an agreement.

WestJet issued its own 72-hour lockout notice in response but struck an optimistic tone later in the day.

"We remain encouraged by the progress we have made in addressing the union's stated priorities. There is no operational impact at this time, and we are optimistic that a tentative agreement can be reached prior to guest travel disruption."

— WestJet statement

The dispute centers on how WestJet compensates its cabin crew. Flight attendants are currently paid through a system of "credit hours" that vary by flight length and do not account for ground delays, de-icing, or other tasks performed before takeoff. CUPE is demanding that crew be paid from the moment they check in until they clock out—a structural change in line with broader efforts by flight attendants across North America.

75,000 Passengers at Risk

Aviation expert John Gradek told CTV News that a full shutdown of WestJet's mainline operations could affect approximately 75,000 passengers. The potential disruption comes during Canada's Civic Holiday long weekend, when domestic air travel volumes peak.

WestJet, which holds roughly 30% of Canada's domestic market share, has offered passengers with flights between July 30 and August 4 the option to rebook or cancel once without penalty. However, travelers who booked through third-party agencies or online travel sites must contact those intermediaries directly—a distinction that could leave some passengers scrambling.

WestJet Encore flights on Q400 aircraft and codeshare flights operated by partner airlines will not be affected by any strike action.

Echoes of Air Canada's 2025 Walkout

The tensions at WestJet follow a pattern of escalating labor disputes in Canadian aviation. Last August, Air Canada flight attendants staged a four-day strike that stranded approximately 500,000 passengers and grounded around 700 daily flights. The Canadian government had intervened to stop the walkout, but Air Canada's flight attendants proceeded anyway—a rare act of defiance that underscored the depth of cabin crew frustration across the industry.

The union has asked the Canadian government not to intervene in the current WestJet negotiations. The office of federal Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu said it expects the two sides "can and should come to an agreement at the bargaining table." A special mediator was appointed earlier this month to assist.

"We've been clear from the start that we want to reach a fair deal without a strike."

— Alia Hussain, President, CUPE Local 8125

What Travelers Should Know

Passengers flying WestJet over the coming days should check their booking contact details and monitor the airline's travel advisory page. Those booked directly with WestJet will receive email updates on any cancellations. WestJet said affected travelers will be refunded or reaccommodated as applicable.

For Indian diaspora travelers, the timing is particularly inconvenient. WestJet operates routes connecting major Canadian cities to the United States and international destinations, and any disruption during the long weekend could cascade through connecting itineraries. With more than 1.8 million people of Indian origin in Canada, many with summer travel plans, the standoff has implications well beyond labor relations.
